That belongs to a different check; the claim that Save isn't seen within about 1 s is not the problem.

Save is still a prominent filled blue button at the end of the form, so findability is not the problem. The real defect on this page is the red '전체 삭제' fused to Save with equal visual weight. That is a destructive-adjacency and misfire issue, covered by the pointing findings, and this finding does not describe it. The model even scores this layout higher (0.11) than the clean layout (0.07), so it is not detecting that hierarchy problem. The claim that the primary is not in the first 4 fixations does not describe a real usability problem for this task.

The measurement is wrong. The 5.2° is to the message centroid, but the #form-errors box (1195-1515 px) ends 12 px left of the Save button. Its nearest point is about 54 px (about 1.3°) from the click, inside even the non-salient 'likely noticed' band under the gaze doc's nearest-point rule. 'Contrast 1.04' compares the pale fill with the page grey (#f3f4f6) and ignores the bold dark-red text. Redundant channels are also present: role=alert, focus moves to the email field, a red 2 px border and an inline error under the field. It is not likely to be missed.

Measurement artefact. #form-errors (x 1195-1515) sits 12 px left of the clicked Save button (x 1527-1611, click at 1569,836). Its near edge is about 54 px (about 1.3°) from the click; the 5.2° is to the centre of a 320 px wide box. 'Non-salient' comes from box contrast 1.04 against a mis-resolved container (#f3f4f6; the card is white). The message is a new object with dark-red text (about 8:1 on #fdecea) and a bold lead. The clean page also shows an inline #email-error, a red 2 px border, and moves focus to the email field. This is recommended error placement, and the message would not plausibly be missed.

The evidence frame is the start screen (snapshot 000), where the full-screen '화면을 탭해서 시작' overlay covers everything. The page exposes no active hotspots in that state; the attack, jump, pause and stick boxes are scenario fallbacks that aren't rendered. Counting #start and the full-screen #view canvas as competitors to an invisible attack button is meaningless. The attributed element and state are both wrong.

Wrong frame. The evidence is S-000, the start screen: the #start overlay covers the viewport, and the game draws no controls at stage 0 (activeHotspots() returns []). The hotspots are scenario-declared 'manual' boxes injected into every snapshot, so a phantom 'attack' is compared with phantom jump/pause/stick plus #start and the canvas #view. In real play the clean attack button is the largest control (92 px, lower right) and clearly dominant.

Snapshot 023 is the supply-target stage. The page's active hotspots there are only stick and pause, and the screenshot shows no attack or jump buttons; the hs-attack box is a scenario fallback. The 'competitors' radar-1 and radar-2 are the task's actual controls at that moment. The primary it claims is out-prioritised does not exist on screen.

S-023 is stage 5 (the '보급 대상 선택' radar panel). The game no longer draws attack or jump at that stage; activeHotspots adds them only for stage <= 3, and the screenshot shows no attack button. The 'primary' is therefore a non-rendered hotspot, while the actual task at that moment is choosing the ally in the radar. Counting radar buttons, the canvas and pause as out-prioritising an invisible control is a mis-measurement.

WCAG 1.4.11 does not require a visible boundary or fill on a button. For an icon-only button, the icon identifies the control, and here it is #374151 on white (about 10:1). The button background is transparent. The 1.02 comes from comparing the light hover tint (#eef2ff) with the page grey, which is not needed to identify the control. At 32x32 px with a clear glyph, this passes the cited standard.

Acceptable under WCAG 1.4.11 and mis-measured. #tools-add is an icon-only button with a transparent fill, and its + icon is #374151 on white (about 10:1). The Understanding doc for 1.4.11 says that if an icon or text is visible and no hit area is indicated, the criterion passes; no boundary is required. The 1.02 comes from S-001/S-002, where the mouse was still hovering: hover background #eef2ff against a mis-resolved container #f3f4f6 gives 1.02 (the card is actually #fff). In S-000 the fill equals the container. This is not a real contrast problem.

The contrast reasoning is the same as the clean variant: the icon glyph is high contrast, and the fill tint is not required by WCAG 1.4.11. This variant does have a real defect on this element, but it is target size (14x14 px with 2 px gaps, a WCAG 2.5.8/PT-01 failure), not boundary contrast. The finding misstates the problem.

Same mechanism as EF-023. The value is the transient hover fill (#eef2ff vs #f3f4f6 = 1.02), not the identifying visual. The icon (#374151 on white, about 10:1) identifies the button, and WCAG 1.4.11 needs no boundary for a visible icon. The genuine defect of this 14x14 px control is its target size, which is reported separately by the pointing checks (EF-009). It is not a boundary-contrast problem.

This one is borderline, but I judged it not meaningful. 14 px at 65 cm is about 20′ em, which clears the ISO 9241-303 16′ minimum and is a mainstream desktop UI size. The 24.6′ Hangul critical print size is snippet-level with an unconfirmed metric, and the Korean MNREAD data suggest young adults' critical print size is lower. The text is a 25-character alert, not continuous reading, so any reading-speed effect is negligible, and the same message is repeated inline at the field. At most a general base-font note, not an element defect.

Correctly measured and attributed. 14 px x 0.2745 mm (23.8-inch 1080p) = 3.84 mm, which is 20.3' at 650 mm. That is below the young Hangul critical print size (24.6', about KRDS's 17 px default at this geometry), well below the older 31.2', and below KRDS's 16 px body guidance. The element is a sentence-level error message (26 chars) that users must read to recover, so it is in the rule's continuous-text scope. The impact is minor: the message is short, the bold inline error repeats it, and the Hangul CPS metric is unconfirmed. P3 is the right severity.

This is misapplied. The text is a Latin e-mail address in a table cell, so the Hangul critical print size does not apply, and it is a data value, not continuous prose where reading speed matters. 14 px table text on a 24-inch 1080p monitor at 65 cm is ordinary and legible.

Out of the rule's scope and mislabelled. The critical-print-size tier applies to continuous reading text only. 'jihoon.park@example.com' is a Latin data value in a table cell, read at a glance rather than as a sentence; only the >= 12-character proxy let it in. The finding also cites the Hangul CPS for Latin text. Small base text could at most be one page-wide note, not a per-cell reading-speed finding.

The baseline miss rate is 1.1%. The 6.4% comes only from an assumed ×1.3 thumb multiplier, which extrapolates beyond the model's fitted range. Pause is an infrequent, non-destructive, instantly retryable secondary control at 44 CSS px (about 8.1 mm), above HIG 44 pt/28 pt and Material 48 dp. A miss lands on inert canvas, because the pointer handler ignores taps outside hotspots. The pointing doc itself rates such controls P3 at most; not a meaningful problem.

Not a meaningful problem; the P2 comes only from an assumed profile multiplier. The baseline miss is 1.1%, below every band; 6.4% is the sigma x1.3 inflation, which is a declared assumption. The target is the pause, a secondary, occasional control never tapped in the run. It is 44 CSS px (8.1 mm), which meets iOS 44 pt and WCAG 2.5.5 AAA 44 px and is only marginally under Material's 48 dp. A miss lands on empty canvas and costs one retap, so this is not 'meaningful extra effort'. The current code caps such non-path, non-primary profile findings at P3.

The pause hotspot is identical to the non-clean variant, so the reasoning is the same. The P2 rests purely on an extrapolated profile multiplier. The control is platform-standard size, secondary and infrequent, and a miss is harmless because it hits inert canvas and the user simply taps again. A careful reviewer would not report it.

Identical pause-button geometry in the clean game (44x44 CSS px at top centre, far from other controls), with the same reasoning as EF-036. The baseline model predicts a 1.1% miss and the 6.4% is purely the assumed sigma x1.3 inflation. It is an infrequent secondary control meeting 44 pt/44 px guidance, and a miss is a harmless retap on the canvas. This does not merit a P2 or a report.
